Line 21: **NOTE:** This playbook supplements the Firm\'s General M&A Playbook (v.7.1) and should be read in conjunction with it. Where this sector-specific playbook addresses a topic also covered in the General Playbook, this playbook governs for environmental services transactions. In the event of any inconsistency between this playbook and the General M&A Playbook with respect to an environmental services acquisition, the guidance set forth in this playbook controls. Associates should maintain copies of both playbooks and consult both when reviewing or drafting transaction documents for environmental services targets.
Line 29: This playbook provides comprehensive guidance to associates at Ashford, Pennington & Yates LLP who are reviewing, drafting, or marking up stock purchase agreements (\"SPAs\") and asset purchase agreements (\"APAs\") on behalf of private equity (\"PE\") buyer clients acquiring companies in the environmental services sector. For purposes of this playbook, \"environmental services\" encompasses a broad range of businesses, including environmental remediation, hazardous waste management, hazardous waste transportation, environmental consulting, environmental engineering, environmental testing and laboratory services, and related businesses.
Line 33: > \(i\) **Significant potential environmental liabilities** under the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act (\"CERCLA\"), the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (\"RCRA\"), and state equivalents, which can result in strict, joint and several liability for contamination at sites where the target has operated, disposed of waste, or arranged for disposal;
Line 35: > \(ii\) **Heavy regulatory permitting requirements**, including permits under RCRA, the Clean Air Act, the Clean Water Act, and various state environmental regulatory programs, many of which are subject to transfer or notification requirements upon a change of control;
Line 37: > \(iii\) **Government contract exposure and anti-assignment rules**, as many environmental services companies derive significant revenue from federal, state, and local government contracts that are subject to the Anti-Assignment Act, Federal Acquisition Regulation (\"FAR\") novation requirements, and similar restrictions;
Line 39: > \(iv\) **Key-person dependencies for professional licenses**, as environmental consulting and engineering businesses often depend on individuals holding professional engineer (\"PE\") licenses, professional geologist licenses, or other professional certifications that are personal to the individual and cannot be transferred; and
Line 41: > \(v\) **Above-market affiliate transactions**, which are common in family-owned or closely held targets and which can distort EBITDA calculations and create ongoing post-closing value leakage if not properly addressed in the acquisition documentation.
Line 47: This playbook is designed for the deal profile most commonly encountered by the firm\'s PE buyer clients in the environmental services sector. The typical transaction parameters are as follows:
Line 49: **Enterprise Value Range.** Middle-market environmental services acquisitions with enterprise values typically ranging from \$75 million to \$500 million. The majority of transactions handled by the firm in this sector fall within the \$100 million to \$350 million range.
Line 51: **Transaction Structure.** 100% stock purchase or asset purchase. Stock purchases are strongly preferred by PE buyers in this sector because a stock acquisition preserves the target entity\'s environmental permits, government contracts, and professional registrations without the need for transfer, novation, or re-issuance. Asset purchases may be required in certain circumstances, such as corporate divestitures where the target business is a division rather than a separate legal entity, or where the buyer wishes to avoid assuming certain liabilities. When an asset purchase structure is used, associates must pay particular attention to environmental permit transfer requirements and government contract assignment restrictions, both of which are more complex in asset deals.
Line 55: **Seller Profile.** The seller is typically a founder-owned or family-owned holding company, a closely held group of shareholders, or a corporate parent divesting a non-core business line. Family-owned sellers are particularly common in the environmental services sector, as many environmental remediation and waste management companies were founded in the 1980s and 1990s during the initial wave of CERCLA enforcement and are now being sold by retiring founders. Associates should be alert to the dynamics of negotiating with founder-sellers, who may have strong emotional attachments to the business and who may insist on provisions that are not market-standard.
Line 57: **Valuation.** Typical EBITDA multiples in the environmental services sector range from 5.5x to 7.5x Adjusted EBITDA, with the precise multiple depending on factors including geographic footprint, customer concentration, regulatory compliance history, government contract backlog, and growth trajectory. Premium multiples (above 7.0x) are typically reserved for targets with significant recurring revenue, diversified customer bases, and strong regulatory track records.
Line 59: **Common EBITDA Adjustments.** The Adjusted EBITDA calculation in environmental services transactions commonly includes adjustments for: (a) above-market rent payments to seller-affiliated entities (which is one of the most significant adjustments in family-owned targets); (b) one-time litigation costs, including environmental litigation defense costs; (c) excess owner compensation (where the founder-owner draws a salary significantly above market for a comparable executive); (d) one-time transaction expenses; and (e) non-recurring regulatory compliance costs. Associates should review the quality of earnings report prepared by the buyer\'s financial advisor and ensure that the EBITDA adjustments reflected in the purchase price are properly addressed in the SPA\'s working capital methodology and affiliate transaction provisions.
Line 61: **Buyer\'s Lender.** In many recent transactions, the buyer\'s acquisition financing has been provided by specialty lenders such as Clearwater Environmental Lending Corp. and similar institutions with sector expertise. These lenders impose additional requirements on deal documentation, including specific insurance requirements, environmental compliance covenants, and reporting obligations. Associates should obtain and review the lender\'s term sheet and commitment letter early in the drafting process and ensure that the SPA\'s closing mechanics, representations, and covenants are consistent with the lender\'s requirements.
Line 67: > \(a\) **The executed term sheet** (or letter of intent), which is always the primary benchmark for the commercial terms of the transaction. Where the term sheet specifies a particular deal term (such as the indemnification cap or non-compete duration), the SPA must conform to the term sheet unless the responsible partner has authorized a deviation.
Line 69: > \(b\) **The due diligence reports**, particularly the environmental due diligence memo, the regulatory compliance memo, and the government contracts memo. These reports identify specific risks that must be addressed in the SPA.
Line 75: **[Section 2: Material Adverse Effect Definition]{.underline}**
Line 77: **[2.1 Firm Standard on MAE Definitions]{.underline}**
Line 79: The Material Adverse Effect (\"MAE\") definition is one of the most heavily negotiated provisions in any acquisition agreement and is critical to the buyer\'s closing conditions and representation structure. The MAE definition determines whether an adverse development at the target between signing and closing constitutes a material adverse change that would permit the buyer to decline to close, and it also qualifies many of the seller\'s representations and warranties (e.g., \"no events have occurred that have had or would reasonably be expected to have a Material Adverse Effect\"). Because of the MAE definition\'s outsized impact on the buyer\'s rights, associates must review it with extreme care.
Line 83: The MAE definition should be narrowly tailored to capture genuine, target-specific material adverse changes in the business, operations, financial condition, assets, liabilities, or results of operations of the target company. The definition should be broad enough to encompass any type of material adverse development, without limiting the concept to a particular category of harm.
Line 85: **Standard Carve-outs.** It is market practice for the MAE definition to include carve-outs (exclusions) for certain categories of changes or events that are beyond the target\'s control and that affect the broader economy or markets rather than the target specifically. The following carve-outs are generally acceptable:
Line 103: **THIS IS A CRITICAL REQUIREMENT.** All industry-specific carve-outs and regulatory carve-outs in the MAE definition MUST include a \"disproportionate impact\" exception. This is a firm-wide requirement and is non-negotiable for environmental services transactions. The standard formulation the firm requires is:
Line 105: > *\"\...provided, however, that any change, effect, event, or development referred to in clauses (a) through (f) above shall be taken into account in determining whether a Material Adverse Effect has occurred or would reasonably be expected to occur to the extent such change, effect, event, or development disproportionately affects the Company and its Subsidiaries, taken as a whole, relative to other participants in the industries in which the Company and its Subsidiaries operate.\"*
Line 107: **Rationale.** Without the disproportionate impact qualifier, industry-specific and regulatory carve-outs can effectively hollow out the MAE definition, rendering it meaningless. This risk is especially acute for environmental services companies. Consider the following scenario: if the MAE definition carves out \"changes in environmental laws or regulations\" or \"changes affecting the environmental services industry generally\" without a disproportionate impact qualifier, the seller could argue that virtually any adverse regulatory development --- including a new CERCLA regulation that specifically targets the target\'s disposal practices, a state-level ban on a waste treatment methodology that constitutes 40% of the target\'s revenue, or an EPA enforcement initiative directed at the specific category of environmental services the target provides --- is excluded from the MAE definition because it \"affects the environmental services industry generally\" or constitutes a \"change in environmental law.\" This interpretation would render the buyer\'s closing condition (no MAE since signing) essentially unenforceable, because the most likely sources of material adverse change for an environmental services company are precisely the regulatory and industry changes that the carve-out would exclude.
Line 109: The disproportionate impact qualifier resolves this problem by providing that even if a change is of the type described in the carve-out (e.g., a general change in environmental law), it still counts toward the MAE analysis to the extent it disproportionately affects the target compared to other industry participants. This preserves the buyer\'s protection against target-specific harm while still excluding truly general, industry-wide developments that affect all participants equally.
Line 111: **Specific Instruction.** If the seller\'s draft excludes \"changes in the environmental services industry generally\" or \"changes in environmental laws or regulations\" from the MAE definition without a disproportionate impact qualifier, this MUST be flagged and corrected. The associate should add the disproportionate impact qualifier language set forth above. **Priority: CRITICAL.**
Line 113: **Example of Acceptable MAE Carve-out Language:**
Line 115: > *\"\...provided, however, that none of the following shall be deemed to constitute, and none of the following shall be taken into account in determining whether there has been, a Material Adverse Effect: (a) changes in general economic conditions or conditions in the financial markets generally; (b) changes affecting the industries in which the Company operates generally; (c) changes in applicable Law (including Environmental Laws) or GAAP; (d) acts of war, armed hostilities, terrorism, or natural disasters; (e) epidemics, pandemics, or other public health emergencies; or (f) changes resulting from the announcement or pendency of the transactions contemplated hereby; provided, further, that, with respect to clauses (a) through (e), such changes, effects, events, or developments may be taken into account in determining whether a Material Adverse Effect has occurred or would reasonably be expected to occur to the extent that such changes, effects, events, or developments have a disproportionate effect on the Company and its Subsidiaries, taken as a whole, relative to other participants in the industries in which the Company and its Subsidiaries operate.\"*
Line 117: **[2.2 Environmental-Sector-Specific MAE Considerations]{.underline}**
Line 119: Beyond the general requirement for the disproportionate impact qualifier addressed in Section 2.1, associates must be attentive to several additional MAE issues that are unique to environmental services acquisitions.
Line 121: **Regulatory Exposure.** Environmental services companies are uniquely exposed to regulatory changes that could devastate the target\'s value. Changes in CERCLA regulations, modifications to RCRA permitting requirements, new EPA enforcement policies, state-level environmental law changes, and shifts in regulatory interpretation can fundamentally alter the target\'s business model, cost structure, and liability exposure. A broadly worded regulatory carve-out without a disproportionate impact qualifier would allow the seller to argue that sweeping regulatory changes affecting the target --- even those directed specifically at the target\'s business practices --- are excluded from the MAE definition. This is precisely the scenario the disproportionate impact qualifier is designed to address, and its importance in the environmental services context cannot be overstated.
Line 123: **Pending or Threatened Litigation.** Associates should carefully review whether the MAE definition carves out \"changes resulting from pending or threatened litigation.\" In many general middle-market transactions, this carve-out is unremarkable. However, for environmental services targets with known environmental exposure --- including targets that are potentially responsible parties (\"PRPs\") at CERCLA Superfund sites, targets with ongoing state environmental enforcement actions, or targets facing private contribution or cost-recovery claims --- a litigation carve-out could exclude from the MAE definition precisely the type of adverse development most likely to occur. If the target has known environmental litigation exposure, the associate should either (a) remove the litigation carve-out entirely, or (b) add an express exclusion to the litigation carve-out providing that it does not apply to environmental litigation or claims arising under CERCLA, RCRA, or state environmental law equivalents.
Line 125: **CERCLA Exposure.** Specifically, exposures of the type associated with CERCLA response cost liability --- such as EPA information requests under CERCLA Section 104(e), PRP notification letters, unilateral administrative orders, and contributions to Superfund remediation costs --- should not be carved out of the MAE definition. These \"Dalton Creek-type\" CERCLA exposures (referring to the category of historical disposal site liabilities frequently encountered in environmental services due diligence) represent some of the most significant and unpredictable risks to environmental services companies, and the buyer must retain the ability to invoke the MAE closing condition if such liabilities materialize or escalate between signing and closing.
Line 127: **Associates should confirm** that the MAE definition, read as a whole, does not inadvertently exclude from the MAE analysis the categories of adverse developments most relevant to the environmental services target being acquired. If in doubt, escalate to the responsible partner.
Line 141: > \(c\) Maintain all insurance policies (including environmental impairment liability insurance) in full force and effect;
Line 145: > \(e\) Comply in all material respects with all applicable laws, permits, and governmental orders;
Line 151: > \(h\) Not make any capital expenditures in excess of an agreed threshold (typically \$250,000 individually or \$500,000 in the aggregate) without buyer\'s prior written consent;
Line 159: > \(l\) Not create, incur, or permit any liens on the Company\'s assets (other than permitted liens); and
Line 163: For environmental services targets, additional sector-specific covenants are required, as set forth in Section 3.3 below. Additionally, affiliate transaction restrictions --- which are critically important in this sector --- are addressed separately in Section 3.2 below.
Line 169: **THIS IS A HIGH-PRIORITY REQUIREMENT.** The interim operating covenants MUST include a specific, express restriction prohibiting the target from entering into, amending, modifying, extending, renewing, or terminating any contract, transaction, or arrangement with the seller, any affiliate of the seller, or any officer, director, manager, member, shareholder, or family member of the seller or any seller affiliate, without the buyer\'s prior written consent (not to be unreasonably withheld, conditioned, or delayed).
Line 171: **Rationale.** In acquisitions of family-owned or closely held environmental services targets, affiliate transactions represent a persistent and significant risk during the Interim Period. The selling shareholders and their affiliated entities frequently engage in transactions with the target that may not be at arm\'s length, and the risk of value extraction through affiliate transactions is heightened during the period between signing and closing, when the seller knows that it will shortly be relinquishing control of the business. Common abuses observed in environmental services transactions handled by the firm include:
Line 173: > \(a\) **Increasing rent payments under affiliate leases.** Environmental services companies frequently lease office space, equipment yards, vehicle storage facilities, or waste disposal facilities from entities controlled by the selling shareholders. The seller may attempt to increase the rent under these leases during the Interim Period, extracting value from the target before the buyer takes control.
Line 175: > \(b\) **Entering into new management or consulting agreements with seller-affiliated entities.** Sellers may attempt to create new contractual payment obligations running from the target to seller affiliates during the Interim Period, often styled as \"management fees,\" \"consulting arrangements,\" or \"transition services.\"
Line 177: > \(c\) **Prepaying obligations to affiliates.** The target may accelerate payment of amounts owed to seller affiliates, depleting the target\'s cash and reducing net working capital.
Line 179: > \(d\) **Extending the term of above-market affiliate contracts.** The seller may attempt to lock in above-market affiliate arrangements for extended periods, making them more difficult or expensive for the buyer to unwind post-closing.
Line 181: **Specific Context for Environmental Services Deals.** In environmental services transactions, it is extremely common for the target to lease critical operational facilities --- including equipment yards, staging areas, waste storage facilities, and disposal sites --- from entities controlled by the selling shareholders. EBITDA adjustments for above-market affiliate rent are among the most common adjustments in this sector, with recent transactions handled by the firm reflecting above-market rent adjustments of \$1,600,000 or more. However, these EBITDA adjustments only protect the buyer on the purchase price (valuation) side --- they do not prevent the seller from increasing or adding affiliate payments during the Interim Period, which would reduce the target\'s cash flow and working capital independent of the valuation adjustment.
Line 183: The affiliate transaction restriction covenant is the primary contractual mechanism to prevent this form of value leakage. Its inclusion in the SPA is mandatory. **Priority: HIGH.**
Line 191: In addition to the general interim operating covenants set forth in Section 3.1 and the affiliate transaction restrictions set forth in Section 3.2, the SPA for an environmental services acquisition must include the following sector-specific interim covenants:
Line 195: > \(b\) **Active Remediation Projects.** Continue all active remediation and environmental response projects in the ordinary course of business and in compliance with all applicable orders, consent decrees, administrative agreements, remediation action plans, and other governmental requirements. Do not voluntarily suspend, terminate, or materially alter the scope of any active remediation project without the buyer\'s prior written consent.
Line 197: > \(c\) **New Environmental Remediation Contracts.** Do not enter into any new environmental remediation or response contract or agreement with a contract value exceeding \$500,000 (or such other threshold as may be agreed) without the buyer\'s prior written consent.
Line 199: > \(d\) **Environmental Insurance.** Maintain all environmental impairment liability insurance policies, pollution legal liability insurance policies, and contractor\'s pollution liability insurance policies in full force and effect, with coverage levels no less than those in effect as of the date of the agreement.
Line 201: > \(e\) **Notice of Environmental Claims.** Provide prompt written notice to the buyer (and in no event later than five (5) business days after the Company\'s receipt thereof) of any new environmental claim, notice of violation, information request under CERCLA Section 104(e), RCRA Section 3007, or any analogous state law provision, consent order, administrative complaint, or other regulatory action received by the Company during the Interim Period.
Line 203: > \(f\) **Settlement of Environmental Claims.** Do not settle, compromise, or consent to the entry of any judgment with respect to any environmental claim, proceeding, or regulatory action involving potential liability in excess of \$250,000 (or such other threshold as may be agreed) without the buyer\'s prior written consent.
Line 205: Associates should review the environmental due diligence memo for a list of all active remediation projects, environmental permits, and pending environmental claims, and confirm that the interim covenants adequately cover each identified item.
Line 213: The firm\'s standard survival framework for PE acquisitions in the environmental services sector is as follows:
Line 215: **Fundamental Representations.** Representations relating to organization and existence, authority and enforceability, capitalization and equity ownership, no conflicts with organizational documents, and brokers and finders fees (collectively, \"Fundamental Representations\") must survive for the longer of (a) the full applicable statute of limitations (including any extensions or tolling periods) or (b) six (6) years post-closing. This survival period is non-negotiable. Fundamental Representations go to the core of the transaction --- whether the seller has the authority to sell what it purports to sell, and whether the buyer is getting what it is paying for. Abbreviated survival periods for Fundamental Representations are never acceptable.
Line 223: **Basket Standard.** For reference (this topic is addressed in detail in Section 5.2), a true deductible of 0.75% to 1.0% of enterprise value is market-standard for middle-market transactions in the environmental services sector. A basket within this range should generally be accepted without markup, as discussed further in Section 11.2.
Line 227: **THIS IS A CRITICAL REQUIREMENT.** For targets in the environmental services sector, environmental representations --- including but not limited to representations regarding environmental compliance, Environmental Permits, hazardous materials and hazardous waste management, CERCLA and Superfund matters, environmental remediation obligations, environmental insurance, and environmental litigation --- MUST survivcation cap under the SPA.
Line 415: **Key Policy Exclusions.** R&W Insurance policies in environmental services transactions typically include exclusions for: (a) known matters (i.e., matters specifically identified in the due diligence process or disclosed on the seller\'s disclosure schedules); (b) environmental liabilities (or, in some cases, sub-limits for environmental liabilities rather than a complete exclusion); (c) specific pre-identified risks flagged by the insurer during underwriting; and (d) forward-looking statements and projections.
Line 417: These exclusions underscore the critical importance of the Special Indemnity provisions described in Section 6. Because the R&W Insurance policy will typically exclude or sub-limit coverage for known environmental liabilities, the seller\'s direct indemnification through the Special Indemnity is the buyer\'s primary source of protection for specifically identified environmental exposures. The R&W Insurance policy and the Special Indemnity serve complementary but distinct functions, and both must be in place.
Line 421: **THIS IS A HIGH-PRIORITY REQUIREMENT.** Where the buyer is obtaining R&W Insurance, the SPA MUST include a provision waiving the R&W insurer\'s subrogation rights against the seller, except in cases of seller fraud.
Line 423: **Standard Formulation.** The SPA should provide that the buyer shall cause the R&W Insurance policy to include a provision waiving the insurer\'s right of subrogation against the seller and its affiliates, directors, officers, employees, and representatives, except to the extent any losses arise from or relate to fraud committed by the seller. The waiver should run to the benefit of the seller and its related parties and should be irrevocable for the term of the policy.
Line 425: **Rationale.** The subrogation waiver is a key commercial term in any R&W Insurance-backed transaction. Without the waiver, the R&W insurer --- after paying a claim to the buyer --- could \"step into the buyer\'s shoes\" and pursue subrogation claims against the seller to recover the amounts paid. This subrogation right would effectively nullify the benefit of R&W Insurance from the seller\'s perspective, because the seller would face the same indemnification exposure (now from the insurer rather than the buyer) that the insurance was supposed to address. The subrogation waiver eliminates this circular liability and is a standard market practice that sellers commonly require as a condition to agreeing to the overall indemnification structure, including the cap, basket, and escrow terms.
Line 427: The exception for fraud preserves the insurer\'s (and the buyer\'s) rights against a seller who has committed fraud in connection with the transaction. A fraudulent seller is not entitled to the benefit of the subrogation waiver, and the insurer should retain full recourse against such a seller.
Line 429: **Specific Instruction.** If the seller\'s draft SPA makes no reference to R&W Insurance or to the waiver of insurer subrogation rights, the associate must add an R&W Insurance subrogation waiver provision. In many transactions, the availability and structure of R&W Insurance is negotiated at the term-sheet level, and the subrogation waiver is a term-sheet-level commitment. Its omission from the SPA must be corrected. **Priority: HIGH.**
Line 433: > *\"Buyer shall obtain and maintain a representations and warranties insurance policy (the \'R&W Insurance Policy\') and shall cause such R&W Insurance Policy to provide that the insurer thereunder shall waive, and shall not exercise or pursue, any right of subrogation or any other right of recovery against Seller or any of its Affiliates, directors, officers, employees, agents, or representatives with respect to any claim made by Buyer under such R&W Insurance Policy, except to the extent such claim arises from or relates to Fraud by Seller. Buyer shall not amend, modify, or waive any provision of the R&W Insurance Policy in a manner that would adversely affect Seller\'s rights under this Section \[\_\_\] without Seller\'s prior written consent.\"*
Line 435: **Coordination with Other Provisions.** The availability of R&W Insurance does not change the SPA\'s indemnification cap, escrow requirements, or other indemnification terms. The R&W Insurance policy is a supplement to the seller\'s direct indemnification obligations, not a substitute for them. Associates should resist any seller argument that the availability of R&W Insurance justifies a lower SPA indemnification cap or a smaller escrow.
Line 441: The SPA must include a standard net working capital (\"NWC\") true-up mechanism to ensure that the target is delivered to the buyer at closing with a normalized level of working capital. The firm\'s standard NWC adjustment mechanics are as follows:
Line 455: The SPA must require the seller to deliver payoff letters from each holder of target indebtedness no later than three (3) business days prior to the scheduled closing date. Each payoff letter must include: (a) the total outstanding balance as of the anticipated closing date (including accrued and unpaid interest, prepayment premiums, breakage costs, and all other amounts necessary to fully satisfy the obligation); (b) wiring instructions for the payoff amount; and (c) an agreement by the lender to deliver lien release documentation (including UCC-3 termination statements, mortgage releases, and intellectual property lien releases, as applicable) promptly upon receipt of the payoff amount.
Line 457: Delivery of payoff letters meeting these requirements should be a condition to the buyer\'s obligation to close. If payoff letters are not delivered timely, the buyer should have the right to delay closing until they are delivered or, if the delay exceeds a specified number of business days, to terminate the agreement.
Line 465: > \(c\) All capital lease obligations (determined in accordance with GAAP);
Line 479: **Lender Coordination.** The buyer\'s acquisition lender (e.g., Clearwater Environmental Lending Corp. or a similar specialty lender) will typically require payoff letters as a condition to funding the acquisition facility. The SPA\'s closing mechanics must align with the lender\'s requirements regarding the timing and content of payoff letters. Associates should obtain and review the buyer\'s lender\'s commitment letter to identify any specific payoff letter requirements and ensure that the SPA\'s closing conditions are consistent.
Line 485: Non-competition and non-solicitation covenants are standard in PE acquisitions and are critical to protecting the buyer\'s investment in the acquired business. A well-drafted non-compete prevents the seller (and its principals) from establishing or participating in a competing business that could divert customers, employees, or business opportunities from the acquired company during the critical post-acquisition integration period.
Line 487: Associates should always cross-reference the executed term sheet for the agreed-upon non-compete parameters (duration, geographic scope, and business scope). The SPA\'s non-compete provisions must conform to the term sheet.
Line 491: **Duration.** Two (2) to four (4) years post-closing. Three (3) years is the most common duration in recent environmental services transactions handled by the firm and is the firm\'s standard recommendation. Durations shorter than two years provide inadequate protection for the buyer\'s investment; durations longer than four years may raise enforceability concerns in certain jurisdictions.
Line 493: **Geographic Scope.** The non-compete should be limited to the states and jurisdictions in which the target conducts business as of the closing date, plus any states or jurisdictions in which the target has active proposals or bids pending as of the closing date. A nationwide non-compete is generally not advisable unless the target operates in a majority of states. An overbroad geographic restriction risks unenforceability --- courts in many jurisdictions will decline to enforce a non-compete with a geographic scope that is not reasonably tailored to the legitimate business interest being protected.
Line 495: **Business Scope.** The non-compete should be limited to the specific business lines of the target --- for example, \"environmental remediation services, hazardous waste management and transportation services, and environmental consulting and engineering services.\" The non-compete should not extend to \"any business\" or to business lines unrelated to the target\'s operations. Where the seller is a diversified holding company with business lines unrelated to the target (e.g., construction, timber management, real estate development), an overbroad non-compete could restrict legitimate seller activities and may be struck down by a court as unreasonable in its scope.
Line 497: **Enforceability Considerations.** Enforceability of non-compete covenants varies significantly by jurisdiction. Delaware courts generally enforce reasonable non-competition covenants entered into in connection with the sale of a business, applying a reasonableness standard that considers the duration, geographic scope, and business scope of the restriction in light of the legitimate interests being protected. Oregon courts similarly apply a reasonableness test but impose specific statutory requirements for non-compete agreements. Some jurisdictions (most notably California) are hostile to non-compete covenants generally, although the sale-of-business exception may apply. Associates should identify the governing law of the non-compete provision and confirm that the covenant\'s terms are consistent with the requirements of that jurisdiction. Overbroad covenants risk being voided entirely rather than judicially reformed, depending on the jurisdiction\'s approach to reformation (sometimes called \"blue penciling\").
Line 499: **Non-Solicitation.** In addition to the non-compete, the SPA should include non-solicitation covenants prohibiting the seller and its principals from (a) soliciting or hiring employees of the target and (b) soliciting or diverting customers or suppliers of the target. The non-solicitation period should match the non-compete period.
Line 507: **Firm Standard.** For targets with fewer than 500 employees (which includes the majority of environmental services targets in the middle-market range), actual knowledge of the Chief Executive Officer and Chief Financial Officer (or their functional equivalents) is an acceptable Knowledge standard. These individuals typically have sufficient familiarity with the target\'s operations, financial condition, regulatory compliance status, and material contracts to provide meaningful knowledge-qualified representations.
Line 515: This section provides guidance on provisions that, while potentially appearing sub-optimal from the buyer\'s perspective, are within acceptable market ranges and should generally NOT be marked up in the seller\'s draft. Disciplined markup is essential to maintaining the credibility of the associate, the responsible partner, and the firm. Marking up provisions that are squarely within market range wastes negotiating capital, creates unnecessary friction, and signals to the seller\'s counsel that the buyer\'s team is either inexperienced or unreasonable.
Line 519: > **Basket/Deductible at 0.75%--1.0% of Enterprise Value.** As discussed in Section 5.2, this is within the firm\'s acceptable range for middle-market environmental services transactions. A basket at 1.0% of enterprise value should not be marked up. Do not attempt to negotiate the basket down to 0.5% or lower merely because a lower basket would be better for the buyer --- the improvement is marginal and the negotiating capital is better spent elsewhere.
Line 533: In a stock acquisition, the target entity itself does not change --- the same legal entity that held the environmental permits before the transaction continues to hold them after the transaction. This is one of the principal advantages of a stock purchase structure for environmental services targets with complex permitting portfolios. However, the mere fact that the permit-holding entity does not change does not mean that the change of control is transparent to regulators.
Line 535: Many state environmental regulatory programs --- including programs authorized under RCRA, the Clean Air Act, and the Clean Water Act --- require notification to, or approval from, the issuing regulatory agency upon a change of control of the permit holder, even in stock purchase transactions. The specific requirements vary by state and by permit type, and failure to comply with applicable notification or approval requirements can result in permit violations, enforcement actions, or, in extreme cases, permit revocation.
Line 537: **States of Particular Note.** Based on the firm\'s recent transaction experience in the environmental services sector, the following states impose change-of-control notification or approval requirements that are particularly relevant:
Line 539: > \(a\) **Oregon:** The Oregon Department of Environmental Quality (\"DEQ\") requires change-of-ownership notifications for certain categories of environmental permits, including RCRA hazardous waste facility permits and water quality permits.
Line 541: > \(b\) **Washington:** The Washington Department of Ecology requires similar notifications and, in some cases, formal approval for changes of ownership affecting certain environmental permits.
Line 543: > \(c\) **California:** The California Department of Toxic Substances Control (\"DTSC\") has specific requirements for notification and, in certain circumstances, prior approval of changes of control for hazardous waste facility permits.
Line 545: > \(d\) **Nevada:** The Nevada Division of Environmental Protection (\"NDEP\") imposes change-of-ownership notification requirements for certain permits.
Line 547: **Firm Standard.** The SPA should include both (a) a representation regarding the current status of all Environmental Permits held by the target (including confirmation that all permits are in full force and effect, that no permit is subject to pending revocation or suspension, and that no conditions exist that could give rise to revocation or suspension) AND (b) pre-closing and post-closing covenants requiring the seller\'s cooperation in the notification, transfer, or re-issuance of Environmental Permits as required by applicable law. The cooperation covenant should extend through a period of at least twelve (12) months post-closing to cover permits with longer regulatory processing timelines.
Line 549: Associates should review the environmental due diligence memo for a comprehensive list of all target permits and should flag any permits that require transfer notifications or regulatory approvals in connection with the change of control.
Line 553: Environmental services companies frequently derive a significant portion of their revenue from government contracts --- including federal, state, and local contracts --- for environmental remediation, environmental consulting, environmental monitoring, and related services. Government contracts present unique legal issues in the acquisition context that associates must address in the SPA.
Line 555: **Federal Government Contracts.** Federal government contracts are subject to the Anti-Assignment Act (41 U.S.C. § 6305), which generally prohibits the assignment of government contracts without the consent of the contracting officer. In addition, FAR 42.12 sets forth the procedures for novation agreements when a contractor undergoes a change of ownership. A novation agreement is a three-party agreement among the government, the original contractor, and the successor contractor, pursuant to which the government recognizes the successor as the contractor under the existing contract.
Line 557: Even in stock purchase transactions --- where the contracting entity does not change --- certain changes in ownership may trigger novation or recognition requirements under FAR. Specifically, FAR 42.1204 provides that a novation agreement may be required when a contractor is acquired by another entity, even if the contractor entity continues to exist. The determination of whether a novation is required depends on the circumstances, including whether the contractor entity remains intact and continues to perform under the contract.
Line 561: > \(i\) A representation regarding the status of all government contracts held by the target, including confirmation that all contracts are in good standing, that no contracts are subject to pending termination for default or convenience, and that no debarment or suspension proceedings are pending or threatened;
Line 563: > \(ii\) A pre-closing covenant requiring the seller and the target to use commercially reasonable efforts to obtain novation or recognition agreements from applicable government contracting officers, to the extent required by applicable law or regulation; and
Line 565: > \(iii\) Consideration of whether government contract consent should be a closing condition. For targets where government contracts represent a material portion of revenue (typically more than 20%), the failure to obtain required novation agreements may justify a closing condition. For targets with a smaller government contract exposure, a pre-closing covenant with commercially reasonable efforts may be sufficient.
Line 567: Associates should cross-reference the government contracts section of the due diligence memo and consult with the firm\'s Government Contracts Practice Group for guidance on specific novation requirements.
Line 575: > \(a\) **Accuracy of Representations and Warranties.** The seller\'s representations and warranties must be true and correct as of the closing date as though made on such date (with appropriate exceptions for representations made as of a specific date). For non-Fundamental Representations, accuracy is qualified by a Material Adverse Effect standard (i.e., the representations must be true and correct except where the failure to be true and correct would not, individually or in the aggregate, reasonably be expected to have a Material Adverse Effect). For Fundamental Representations, accuracy must be true and correct in all respects (other than de minimis inaccuracies).
Line 579: > \(c\) **No Material Adverse Effect.** No Material Adverse Effect shall have occurred since the date of the agreement.
Line 603: In addition to the standard closing conditions set forth in Section 13.1, the following sector-specific closing conditions should be included in environmental services acquisitions where applicable:
Line 605: > \(a\) **Government Contract Novation or Recognition.** Where the target holds material government contracts that require novation or recognition agreements in connection with the change of control, the receipt of such novation or recognition agreements (or, at minimum, written confirmation from the applicable contracting officer that the novation process is underway and that interim performance will be permitted) should be a closing condition. See Section 12.2 for further guidance.
Line 607: > \(b\) **Environmental Permit Transfer Notifications.** Where applicable state law requires notification to or approval from a regulatory agency in connection with a change of control of the permit holder, confirmation that all required notifications have been filed (and, where prior approval is required, that such approval has been obtained) should be a closing condition. See Section 12.1 for further guidance.
