matches.line: **NOTE:** This playbook supplements the Firm\'s General M&A Playbook (v.7.1) and should be read in conjunction with it. Where this sector-specific playbook addresses a topic also covered in the General Playbook, this playbook governs for environmental services transactions. In the event of any inconsistency between this playbook and the General M&A Playbook with respect to an environmental services acquisition, the guidance set forth in this playbook controls. Associates should maintain copies of both playbooks and consult both when reviewing or drafting transaction documents for environmental services targets.

This playbook provides comprehensive guidance to associates at Ashford, Pennington & Yates LLP who are reviewing, drafting, or marking up stock purchase agreements (\"SPAs\") and asset purchase agreements (\"APAs\") on behalf of private equity (\"PE\") buyer clients acquiring companies in the environmental services sector. For purposes of this playbook, \"environmental services\" encompasses a broad range of businesses, including environmental remediation, hazardous waste management, hazardous waste transportation, environmental consulting, environmental engineering, environmental testing and laboratory services, and related businesses.

> \(i\) **Significant potential environmental liabilities** under the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act (\"CERCLA\"), the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (\"RCRA\"), and state equivalents, which can result in strict, joint and several liability for contamination at sites where the target has operated, disposed of waste, or arranged for disposal;

> \(ii\) **Heavy regulatory permitting requirements**, including permits under RCRA, the Clean Air Act, the Clean Water Act, and various state environmental regulatory programs, many of which are subject to transfer or notification requirements upon a change of control;

> \(iii\) **Government contract exposure and anti-assignment rules**, as many environmental services companies derive significant revenue from federal, state, and local government contracts that are subject to the Anti-Assignment Act, Federal Acquisition Regulation (\"FAR\") novation requirements, and similar restrictions;

> \(iv\) **Key-person dependencies for professional licenses**, as environmental consulting and engineering businesses often depend on individuals holding professional engineer (\"PE\") licenses, professional geologist licenses, or other professional certifications that are personal to the individual and cannot be transferred; and

> \(v\) **Above-market affiliate transactions**, which are common in family-owned or closely held targets and which can distort EBITDA calculations and create ongoing post-closing value leakage if not properly addressed in the acquisition documentation.
This playbook is designed for the deal profile most commonly encountered by the firm\'s PE buyer clients in the environmental services sector. The typical transaction parameters are as follows:

**Enterprise Value Range.** Middle-market environmental services acquisitions with enterprise values typically ranging from \$75 million to \$500 million. The majority of transactions handled by the firm in this sector fall within the \$100 million to \$350 million range.

**Transaction Structure.** 100% stock purchase or asset purchase. Stock purchases are strongly preferred by PE buyers in this sector because a stock acquisition preserves the target entity\'s environmental permits, government contracts, and professional registrations without the need for transfer, novation, or re-issuance. Asset purchases may be required in certain circumstances, such as corporate divestitures where the target business is a division rather than a separate legal entity, or where the buyer wishes to avoid assuming certain liabilities. When an asset purchase structure is used, associates must pay particular attention to environmental permit transfer requirements and government contract assignment restrictions, both of which are more complex in asset deals.

**Seller Profile.** The seller is typically a founder-owned or family-owned holding company, a closely held group of shareholders, or a corporate parent divesting a non-core business line. Family-owned sellers are particularly common in the environmental services sector, as many environmental remediation and waste management companies were founded in the 1980s and 1990s during the initial wave of CERCLA enforcement and are now being sold by retiring founders. Associates should be alert to the dynamics of negotiating with founder-sellers, who may have strong emotional attachments to the business and who may insist on provisions that are not market-standard.

**Valuation.** Typical EBITDA multiples in the environmental services sector range from 5.5x to 7.5x Adjusted EBITDA, with the precise multiple depending on factors including geographic footprint, customer concentration, regulatory compliance history, government contract backlog, and growth trajectory. Premium multiples (above 7.0x) are typically reserved for targets with significant recurring revenue, diversified customer bases, and strong regulatory track records.

**Common EBITDA Adjustments.** The Adjusted EBITDA calculation in environmental services transactions commonly includes adjustments for: (a) above-market rent payments to seller-affiliated entities (which is one of the most significant adjustments in family-owned targets); (b) one-time litigation costs, including environmental litigation defense costs; (c) excess owner compensation (where the founder-owner draws a salary significantly above market for a comparable executive); (d) one-time transaction expenses; and (e) non-recurring regulatory compliance costs. Associates should review the quality of earnings report prepared by the buyer\'s financial advisor and ensure that the EBITDA adjustments reflected in the purchase price are properly addressed in the SPA\'s working capital methodology and affiliate transaction provisions.

**Buyer\'s Lender.** In many recent transactions, the buyer\'s acquisition financing has been provided by specialty lenders such as Clearwater Environmental Lending Corp. and similar institutions with sector expertise. These lenders impose additional requirements on deal documentation, including specific insurance requirements, environmental compliance covenants, and reporting obligations. Associates should obtain and review the lender\'s term sheet and commitment letter early in the drafting process and ensure that the SPA\'s closing mechanics, representations, and covenants are consistent with the lender\'s requirements.

> \(a\) **The executed term sheet** (or letter of intent), which is always the primary benchmark for the commercial terms of the transaction. Where the term sheet specifies a particular deal term (such as the indemnification cap or non-compete duration), the SPA must conform to the term sheet unless the responsible partner has authorized a deviation.

> \(b\) **The due diligence reports**, particularly the environmental due diligence memo, the regulatory compliance memo, and the government contracts memo. These reports identify specific risks that must be addressed in the SPA.
**[Section 2: Material Adverse Effect Definition]{.underline}**
**[2.1 Firm Standard on MAE Definitions]{.underline}**

The Material Adverse Effect (\"MAE\") definition is one of the most heavily negotiated provisions in any acquisition agreement and is critical to the buyer\'s closing conditions and representation structure. The MAE definition determines whether an adverse development at the target between signing and closing constitutes a material adverse change that would permit the buyer to decline to close, and it also qualifies many of the seller\'s representations and warranties (e.g., \"no events have occurred that have had or would reasonably be expected to have a Material Adverse Effect\"). Because of the MAE definition\'s outsized impact on the buyer\'s rights, associates must review it with extreme care.

The MAE definition should be narrowly tailored to capture genuine, target-specific material adverse changes in the business, operations, financial condition, assets, liabilities, or results of operations of the target company. The definition should be broad enough to encompass any type of material adverse development, without limiting the concept to a particular category of harm.

**Standard Carve-outs.** It is market practice for the MAE definition to include carve-outs (exclusions) for certain categories of changes or events that are beyond the target\'s control and that affect the broader economy or markets rather than the target specifically. The following carve-outs are generally acceptable:

**THIS IS A CRITICAL REQUIREMENT.** All industry-specific carve-outs and regulatory carve-outs in the MAE definition MUST include a \"disproportionate impact\" exception. This is a firm-wide requirement and is non-negotiable for environmental services transactions. The standard formulation the firm requires is:

> *\"\...provided, however, that any change, effect, event, or development referred to in clauses (a) through (f) above shall be taken into account in determining whether a Material Adverse Effect has occurred or would reasonably be expected to occur to the extent such change, effect, event, or development disproportionately affects the Company and its Subsidiaries, taken as a whole, relative to other participants in the industries in which the Company and its Subsidiaries operate.\"*

**Rationale.** Without the disproportionate impact qualifier, industry-specific and regulatory carve-outs can effectively hollow out the MAE definition, rendering it meaningless. This risk is especially acute for environmental services companies. Consider the following scenario: if the MAE definition carves out \"changes in environmental laws or regulations\" or \"changes affecting the environmental services industry generally\" without a disproportionate impact qualifier, the seller could argue that virtually any adverse regulatory development --- including a new CERCLA regulation that specifically targets the target\'s disposal practices, a state-level ban on a waste treatment methodology that constitutes 40% of the target\'s revenue, or an EPA enforcement initiative directed at the specific category of environmental services the target provides --- is excluded from the MAE definition because it \"affects the environmental services industry generally\" or constitutes a \"change in environmental law.\" This interpretation would render the buyer\'s closing condition (no MAE since signing) essentially unenforceable, because the most likely sources of material adverse change for an environmental services company are precisely the regulatory and industry changes that the carve-out would exclude.

The disproportionate impact qualifier resolves this problem by providing that even if a change is of the type described in the carve-out (e.g., a general change in environmental law), it still counts toward the MAE analysis to the extent it disproportionately affects the target compared to other industry participants. This preserves the buyer\'s protection against target-specific harm while still excluding truly general, industry-wide developments that affect all participants equally.

**Specific Instruction.** If the seller\'s draft excludes \"changes in the environmental services industry generally\" or \"changes in environmental laws or regulations\" from the MAE definition without a disproportionate impact qualifier, this MUST be flagged and corrected. The associate should add the disproportionate impact qualifier language set forth above. **Priority: CRITICAL.**
**Example of Acceptable MAE Carve-out Language:**

> *\"\...provided, however, that none of the following shall be deemed to constitute, and none of the following shall be taken into account in determining whether there has been, a Material Adverse Effect: (a) changes in general economic conditions or conditions in the financial markets generally; (b) changes affecting the industries in which the Company operates generally; (c) changes in applicable Law (including Environmental Laws) or GAAP; (d) acts of war, armed hostilities, terrorism, or natural disasters; (e) epidemics, pandemics, or other public health emergencies; or (f) changes resulting from the announcement or pendency of the transactions contemplated hereby; provided, further, that, with respect to clauses (a) through (e), such changes, effects, events, or developments may be taken into account in determining whether a Material Adverse Effect has occurred or would reasonably be expected to occur to the extent that such changes, effects, events, or developments have a disproportionate effect on the Company and its Subsidiaries, taken as a whole, relative to other participants in the industries in which the Company and its Subsidiaries operate.\"*
**[2.2 Environmental-Sector-Specific MAE Considerations]{.underline}**

Beyond the general requirement for the disproportionate impact qualifier addressed in Section 2.1, associates must be attentive to several additional MAE issues that are unique to environmental services acquisitions.

**Regulatory Exposure.** Environmental services companies are uniquely exposed to regulatory changes that could devastate the target\'s value. Changes in CERCLA regulations, modifications to RCRA permitting requirements, new EPA enforcement policies, state-level environmental law changes, and shifts in regulatory interpretation can fundamentally alter the target\'s business model, cost structure, and liability exposure. A broadly worded regulatory carve-out without a disproportionate impact qualifier would allow the seller to argue that sweeping regulatory changes affecting the target --- even those directed specifically at the target\'s business practices --- are excluded from the MAE definition. This is precisely the scenario the disproportionate impact qualifier is designed to address, and its importance in the environmental services context cannot be overstated.

**Pending or Threatened Litigation.** Associates should carefully review whether the MAE definition carves out \"changes resulting from pending or threatened litigation.\" In many general middle-market transactions, this carve-out is unremarkable. However, for environmental services targets with known environmental exposure --- including targets that are potentially responsible parties (\"PRPs\") at CERCLA Superfund sites, targets with ongoing state environmental enforcement actions, or targets facing private contribution or cost-recovery claims --- a litigation carve-out could exclude from the MAE definition precisely the type of adverse development most likely to occur. If the target has known environmental litigation exposure, the associate should either (a) remove the litigation carve-out entirely, or (b) add an express exclusion to the litigation carve-out providing that it does not apply to environmental litigation or claims arising under CERCLA, RCRA, or state environmental law equivalents.

**CERCLA Exposure.** Specifically, exposures of the type associated with CERCLA response cost liability --- such as EPA information requests under CERCLA Section 104(e), PRP notification letters, unilateral administrative orders, and contributions to Superfund remediation costs --- should not be carved out of the MAE definition. These \"Dalton Creek-type\" CERCLA exposures (referring to the category of historical disposal site liabilities frequently encountered in environmental services due diligence) represent some of the most significant and unpredictable risks to environmental services companies, and the buyer must retain the ability to invoke the MAE closing condition if such liabilities materialize or escalate between signing and closing.

**Associates should confirm** that the MAE definition, read as a whole, does not inadvertently exclude from the MAE analysis the categories of adverse developments most relevant to the environmental services target being acquired. If in doubt, escalate to the responsible partner.
> \(c\) Maintain all insurance policies (including environmental impairment liability insurance) in full force and effect;
> \(e\) Comply in all material respects with all applicable laws, permits, and governmental orders;
> \(h\) Not make any capital expenditures in excess of an agreed threshold (typically \$250,000 individually or \$500,000 in the aggregate) without buyer\'s prior written consent;
> \(l\) Not create, incur, or permit any liens on the Company\'s assets (other than permitted liens); and

For environmental services targets, additional sector-specific covenants are required, as set forth in Section 3.3 below. Additionally, affiliate transaction restrictions --- which are critically important in this sector --- are addressed separately in Section 3.2 below.

**THIS IS A HIGH-PRIORITY REQUIREMENT.** The interim operating covenants MUST include a specific, express restriction prohibiting the target from entering into, amending, modifying, extending, renewing, or terminating any contract, transaction, or arrangement with the seller, any affiliate of the seller, or any officer, director, manager, member, shareholder, or family member of the seller or any seller affiliate, without the buyer\'s prior written consent (not to be unreasonably withheld, conditioned, or delayed).

**Rationale.** In acquisitions of family-owned or closely held environmental services targets, affiliate transactions represent a persistent and significant risk during the Interim Period. The selling shareholders and their affiliated entities frequently engage in transactions with the target that may not be at arm\'s length, and the risk of value extraction through affiliate transactions is heightened during the period between signing and closing, when the seller knows that it will shortly be relinquishing control of the business. Common abuses observed in environmental services transactions handled by the firm include:

> \(a\) **Increasing rent payments under affiliate leases.** Environmental services companies frequently lease office space, equipment yards, vehicle storage facilities, or waste disposal facilities from entities controlled by the selling shareholders. The seller may attempt to increase the rent under these leases during the Interim Period, extracting value from the target before the buyer takes control.

> \(b\) **Entering into new management or consulting agreements with seller-affiliated entities.** Sellers may attempt to create new contractual payment obligations running from the target to seller affiliates during the Interim Period, often styled as \"management fees,\" \"consulting arrangements,\" or \"transition services.\"
> \(c\) **Prepaying obligations to affiliates.** The target may accelerate payment of amounts owed to seller affiliates, depleting the target\'s cash and reducing net working capital.

> \(d\) **Extending the term of above-market affiliate contracts.** The seller may attempt to lock in above-market affiliate arrangements for extended periods, making them more difficult or expensive for the buyer to unwind post-closing.

**Specific Context for Environmental Services Deals.** In environmental services transactions, it is extremely common for the target to lease critical operational facilities --- including equipment yards, staging areas, waste storage facilities, and disposal sites --- from entities controlled by the selling shareholders. EBITDA adjustments for above-market affiliate rent are among the most common adjustments in this sector, with recent transactions handled by the firm reflecting above-market rent adjustments of \$1,600,000 or more. However, these EBITDA adjustments only protect the buyer on the purchase price (valuation) side --- they do not prevent the seller from increasing or adding affiliate payments during the Interim Period, which would reduce the target\'s cash flow and working capital independent of the valuation adjustment.
The affiliate transaction restriction covenant is the primary contractual mechanism to prevent this form of value leakage. Its inclusion in the SPA is mandatory. **Priority: HIGH.**

In addition to the general interim operating covenants set forth in Section 3.1 and the affiliate transaction restrictions set forth in Section 3.2, the SPA for an environmental services acquisition must include the following sector-specific interim covenants:

> \(b\) **Active Remediation Projects.** Continue all active remediation and environmental response projects in the ordinary course of business and in compliance with all applicable orders, consent decrees, administrative agreements, remediation action plans, and other governmental requirements. Do not voluntarily suspend, terminate, or materially alter the scope of any active remediation project without the buyer\'s prior written consent.

> \(c\) **New Environmental Remediation Contracts.** Do not enter into any new environmental remediation or response contract or agreement with a contract value exceeding \$500,000 (or such other threshold as may be agreed) without the buyer\'s prior written consent.

> \(d\) **Environmental Insurance.** Maintain all environmental impairment liability insurance policies, pollution legal liability insurance policies, and contractor\'s pollution liability insurance policies in full force and effect, with coverage levels no less than those in effect as of the date of the agreement.

> \(e\) **Notice of Environmental Claims.** Provide prompt written notice to the buyer (and in no event later than five (5) business days after the Company\'s receipt thereof) of any new environmental claim, notice of violation, information request under CERCLA Section 104(e), RCRA Section 3007, or any analogous state law provision, consent order, administrative complaint, or other regulatory action received by the Company during the Interim Period.

> \(f\) **Settlement of Environmental Claims.** Do not settle, compromise, or consent to the entry of any judgment with respect to any environmental claim, proceeding, or regulatory action involving potential liability in excess of \$250,000 (or such other threshold as may be agreed) without the buyer\'s prior written consent.

Associates should review the environmental due diligence memo for a list of all active remediation projects, environmental permits, and pending environmental claims, and confirm that the interim covenants adequately cover each identified item.
The firm\'s standard survival framework for PE acquisitions in the environmental services sector is as follows:

**Fundamental Representations.** Representations relating to organization and existence, authority and enforceability, capitalization and equity ownership, no conflicts with organizational documents, and brokers and finders fees (collectively, \"Fundamental Representations\") must survive for the longer of (a) the full applicable statute of limitations (including any extensions or tolling periods) or (b) six (6) years post-closing. This survival period is non-negotiable. Fundamental Representations go to the core of the transaction --- whether the seller has the authority to sell what it purports to sell, and whether the buyer is getting what it is paying for. Abbreviated survival periods for Fundamental Representations are never acceptable.

**Basket Standard.** For reference (this topic is addressed in detail in Section 5.2), a true deductible of 0.75% to 1.0% of enterprise value is market-standard for middle-market transactions in the environmental services sector. A basket within this range should generally be accepted without markup, as discussed further in Section 11.2.

**THIS IS A CRITICAL REQUIREMENT.** For targets in the environmental services sector, environmental representations --- including but not limited to representations regarding environmental compliance, Environmental Permits, hazardous materials and hazardous waste management, CERCLA and Superfund matters, environmental remediation obligations, environmental insurance, and environmental litigation --- MUST survive for a minimum of thirty-six (36) months post-closing. The firm\'s preferred position is survival for the full applicable statute of limitations (which, for CERCLA claims, is effectively indefinite, as CERCLA imposes strict, joint and several liability with no statute of repose in many circumstances).

**Rationale.** Environmental liabilities under CERCLA, RCRA, and state environmental law equivalents frequently take years --- and in some cases, decades --- to manifest fully. The lifecycle of a typical CERCLA enforcement action illustrates this point:

Given this timeline, a twelve-month survival period for environmental representations in an environmental services acquisition is grossly inadequate and well below market expectations for this sector. A buyer who discovers a previously undisclosed CERCLA exposure fifteen months after closing --- a timeline that is entirely typical --- would have no indemnification recourse under a twelve-month survival provision. This outcome is unacceptable for PE buyer clients and does not reflect the risk profile of the sector.

**Specific Instruction.** If the seller\'s draft provides for a general twelve-month or shorter survival period that applies to environmental representations without differentiation, this MUST be flagged and corrected. At minimum, environmental representations should be carved out of the general representation survival period and given an independent survival period of thirty-six (36) months post-closing. Ideally, push for survival for the full applicable statute of limitations. If the seller resists the full statute of limitations, thirty-six months is the firm\'s minimum acceptable position. **Priority: CRITICAL.**

**Coordination with Escrow Release.** The environmental representation survival period must be coordinated with the escrow release schedule (see Section 5.4 below). Escrow funds designated for environmental representation claims should not be released before the expiration of the environmental representation survival period. If the general escrow is scheduled for release at eighteen (18) months post-closing but the environmental representation survival extends to thirty-six (36) months, the SPA must provide for a separate environmental escrow holdback that is maintained through the thirty-sixth month (less any amounts reserved for pending claims).

**Coordination with Special Indemnity.** The environmental representation survival period is separate from and in addition to the Special Indemnity for known environmental liabilities (see Section 6 below). The Special Indemnity addresses specifically identified environmental matters with a separate seventy-two (72) month survival period. The environmental representation survival period addresses breaches of the environmental representations generally --- i.e., undisclosed environmental liabilities and inaccuracies in the environmental representations that are not covered by the Special Indemnity.
**THIS IS A CRITICAL REQUIREMENT.** The general indemnification cap is one of the most significant economic terms in the SPA and must conform precisely to the executed term sheet.

**Firm Standard.** For middle-market PE acquisitions in the \$100 million to \$500 million enterprise value range, the general indemnification cap should be set at 10% to 15% of the base enterprise value. The firm\'s target for PE buyer clients is 12.5% of enterprise value. This percentage represents the firm\'s standard recommendation based on extensive experience in environmental services transactions and is consistent with prevailing market data for the sector.

**Key Instruction.** Associates must always cross-reference the executed term sheet for the agreed-upon indemnification cap percentage. The term sheet is the governing benchmark for all commercial terms, and the indemnification cap is among the most carefully negotiated terms at the LOI stage. If the seller\'s draft SPA sets the general indemnification cap at a percentage different from what was agreed in the term sheet, this MUST be flagged immediately and corrected to match the term sheet. Do not accept any deviation from the term sheet cap without express written authorization from the responsible partner. This is a **Critical** priority item.

For example, if the term sheet specifies a general indemnification cap of 12.5% of enterprise value for a transaction with a \$200 million enterprise value, the SPA\'s general indemnification cap should be \$25,000,000. If the seller\'s draft sets the cap at \$20,000,000 (10% of enterprise value), the associate must flag this as a deviation from the term sheet and mark up the draft to reflect the agreed \$25,000,000 cap.

**R&W Insurance Considerations.** In transactions where the buyer is obtaining representations and warranties insurance (see Section 8), the indemnification cap may be subject to additional negotiation dynamics. The R&W insurer may require a certain retention level (the amount of loss the buyer must bear before the policy responds), which interacts with the SPA\'s basket/deductible and cap structure. However, the SPA cap itself must conform to the term sheet regardless of the R&W Insurance structure. The R&W Insurance policy supplements the seller\'s indemnification obligations --- it does not replace them, and the availability of insurance does not justify a reduction in the SPA cap below the term sheet level.

**Market Data.** In recent environmental services transactions handled by the firm, general indemnification caps have ranged from 10% to 15% of enterprise value. The 12.5% figure is squarely within the market range and represents the firm\'s standard recommendation for PE buyers in this sector. Caps below 10% of enterprise value are below market for environmental services acquisitions and should not be accepted without partner authorization. Caps at the higher end of the range (15%) may be appropriate for transactions with elevated environmental risk profiles.

**Escrow Mechanics.** The escrow amount (typically 7.5% of enterprise value --- see Section 5.4 for details) does NOT limit the buyer\'s right to recover under the indemnification provisions. For non-Fundamental Representation claims, the escrow is the first source of recovery, but the buyer\'s right to indemnification extends to the full amount of the general cap. Claims exceeding the escrow may be pursued directly against the seller (or, in the case of an equity rollover, may be offset against future payments) up to the general cap amount. The SPA must clearly and unambiguously state that the escrow does not constitute a limitation on the buyer\'s indemnification rights and that the buyer may pursue claims directly against the seller for amounts exceeding the escrow balance, up to the general indemnification cap. Any language in the seller\'s draft that could be interpreted as limiting the buyer\'s recovery to the escrow amount must be struck.

**Firm Standard.** A true deductible (not a tipping basket) of 0.75% to 1.0% of enterprise value is the market standard for middle-market transactions in the environmental services sector. Under a true deductible structure, the buyer bears the first dollar of indemnifiable losses up to the deductible amount; once the aggregate losses exceed the deductible, the buyer recovers only the excess over the deductible amount (not the full amount of losses from the first dollar). This is distinguished from a \"tipping basket\" (also called a \"threshold\" or \"first dollar\" basket), under which the basket functions as a threshold --- once aggregate losses exceed the basket amount, the buyer recovers the full amount of losses from the first dollar.
> \(c\) Special Indemnities for known environmental liabilities (see Section 6); and

**THIS IS A CRITICAL REQUIREMENT.** The SPA MUST contain an express pro-sandbagging provision. The firm\'s standard is that the buyer\'s right to indemnification under the agreement shall not be limited, diminished, or otherwise affected by any investigation, due diligence review, or knowledge obtained by or on behalf of the buyer before or after the closing, regardless of whether such knowledge was obtained before or after the execution of the agreement.

**Specific Instruction.** If the seller\'s draft contains an anti-sandbagging provision --- i.e., language providing that the buyer cannot recover for breaches of representations of which the buyer had \"Knowledge\" as of the closing date, or language providing that the buyer\'s indemnification rights are limited to the extent the buyer \"did not know\" of the breach prior to closing --- this language MUST be struck in its entirety and replaced with affirmative pro-sandbagging language. **Priority: CRITICAL.**

**Rationale.** In private equity acquisitions, the buyer conducts extensive due diligence through financial, legal, environmental, regulatory, and operational workstreams. Through this process, the buyer may become aware of potential representation breaches prior to closing --- for example, the environmental due diligence may reveal a potential CERCLA exposure that was not fully disclosed by the seller, or the legal due diligence may identify a non-compliance issue that arguably constitutes a breach of the environmental compliance representation.

An anti-sandbagging clause would penalize the buyer for conducting thorough due diligence by stripping the buyer of indemnification rights with respect to matters discovered during diligence. This creates a perverse incentive for the buyer to limit its own diligence, which is contrary to prudent deal practice and contrary to the interests of both parties (since thorough diligence benefits the transaction by identifying and addressing issues before closing).

More fundamentally, the buyer\'s right to rely on the seller\'s representations and warranties as a contractual allocation of risk is independent of what the buyer discovers during due diligence. The seller\'s representations serve as the seller\'s contractual commitment that certain facts are true and as the seller\'s assumption of the risk of indemnification if those facts prove to be untrue. This risk allocation is a core element of the purchase price negotiation --- the buyer is paying a price that reflects, among other things, the seller\'s representations about the state of the business. An anti-sandbagging clause would shift this risk allocation by relieving the seller of its indemnification obligation whenever the buyer independently discovers the breach, which fundamentally undermines the bargained-for indemnification structure.

**Delaware Law.** Delaware law does not impose a clear default rule on sandbagging. Unlike some jurisdictions that apply a common-law anti-sandbagging rule (under which a buyer\'s pre-closing knowledge of a breach may bar recovery), Delaware courts have not definitively adopted either a pro-sandbagging or anti-sandbagging default rule. This uncertainty makes contractual clarity essential. By including an express pro-sandbagging provision, the parties eliminate any ambiguity about the buyer\'s right to recover regardless of pre-closing knowledge.

> *\"The right to indemnification or other remedy based on the representations, warranties, covenants, and obligations set forth in this Agreement shall not be affected by any investigation conducted by or on behalf of Buyer or any knowledge acquired (or capable of being acquired) by Buyer at any time, whether before or after the execution and delivery of this Agreement or the Closing Date, with respect to the accuracy or inaccuracy of, or compliance with, any such representation, warranty, covenant, or obligation. No claim for indemnification under this Article \[\_\_\] shall be defeated or diminished by reason of any investigation, knowledge, or notice of Buyer, whether before or after the date hereof, and regardless of whether such investigation, knowledge, or notice was available to or obtained by Buyer prior to or after the Closing.\"*

**Escrow Amount.** The standard escrow amount for environmental services acquisitions is 7.5% to 10% of enterprise value. The escrow agent should be an independent trust company with experience in M&A escrow administration (e.g., Pinnacle Trust Company, N.A. or a similar institutional fiduciary). The escrow agent should not be an affiliate of either party or of the buyer\'s lender.

> \(b\) **Fundamental Representations and Special Indemnity Escrow.** Released thirty-six (36) months post-closing, less any amounts reserved for pending and unresolved claims as of the release date. This extended hold period corresponds to the minimum environmental representation survival period and the extended escrow for Special Indemnity claims.

**Escrow Does Not Limit Recovery.** As noted in Section 5.1, the escrow does not limit the buyer\'s indemnification rights. It is a source of funds for the buyer\'s convenience and security, not a cap on recovery. The SPA must clearly state this principle, and the escrow agreement must be consistent with it.

**THIS IS A CRITICAL REQUIREMENT.** Where due diligence has identified a specific, known environmental liability --- such as a pending or threatened CERCLA claim, an EPA information request under CERCLA Section 104(e), a state environmental enforcement action, an ongoing remediation obligation, or any other identified environmental matter --- and the estimated potential liability is \$1,000,000 or more, the SPA MUST include a \"Special Indemnity\" provision for that specific liability.

**Survival.** The Special Indemnity must survive for seventy-two (72) months (six years) post-closing. This extended survival period reflects the long-tail nature of CERCLA and environmental enforcement actions, which --- as discussed in Section 4.2 --- often take years to progress from initial inquiry to resolution. A seventy-two month survival period provides the buyer with a meaningful window within which to assert claims as the environmental matter develops and the buyer\'s actual losses become ascertainable.

**Not Subject to the Basket/Deductible.** The Special Indemnity is a dollar-one indemnification obligation. It is not subject to the general deductible described in Section 5.2. The rationale is straightforward: the basket/deductible is designed to filter out immaterial or de minimis claims arising from general representation breaches. A known environmental liability with an estimated exposure of \$1,000,000 or more is, by definition, not immaterial --- it is a specifically identified risk that has been factored into the purchase price negotiation and that requires dedicated indemnification protection.

**Not Subject to the General Cap.** The Special Indemnity is not counted toward the general indemnification cap described in Section 5.1. It operates as a separate, independent indemnification obligation with its own limitations. The Special Indemnity may be subject to its own sub-cap, which is negotiated on a matter-specific basis and typically reflects the high end of the estimated liability range identified in the environmental due diligence. For example, if the estimated liability range for a CERCLA exposure is \$1,500,000 to \$6,000,000, the Special Indemnity sub-cap might be negotiated at \$6,000,000 or \$7,500,000 (the high end of the range plus a reasonable buffer).

**Specific Identification.** The Special Indemnity provision must specifically identify the environmental matter by name, site location, applicable regulatory proceeding number (if any), nature of the liability (e.g., \"CERCLA response cost liability arising from historical disposal at \[Site Name\]\"), and the specific representation or due diligence finding that identified the matter. The identified matters should be listed on a dedicated schedule to the SPA (typically a \"Schedule of Scheduled Environmental Matters\" or similar title).
**Rationale.** Known environmental liabilities are not appropriately covered by general representation and warranty indemnification for several reasons:

> \(i\) Known environmental matters are already disclosed (and, in many cases, scheduled as exceptions to the environmental representations). Because they are disclosed, they may not technically constitute \"breaches\" of the representations in the traditional sense, potentially leaving the buyer without a general indemnification claim.

> \(ii\) General survival periods (whether eighteen months for general representations or even thirty-six months for environmental representations) are inadequate for the long-tail nature of many environmental enforcement actions, which may take five to ten years to resolve.

> \(iii\) The basket/deductible could prevent recovery for environmental matters falling within the lower end of the estimated liability range, particularly where the buyer has other general indemnification claims consuming the deductible.
> \(iv\) The general indemnification cap may be consumed by other claims, leaving the buyer unprotected for the specific known liability that was the subject of purchase price negotiation.

**Specific Instruction.** If environmental due diligence has identified a known CERCLA exposure --- such as a pending EPA information request at a specific disposal facility --- with an estimated liability range of \$1,500,000 to \$6,000,000, the associate MUST ensure that the SPA contains a Special Indemnity provision specifically covering that exposure. If the seller\'s draft SPA fails to include such a provision, the associate should draft and insert a Special Indemnity provision and raise it with the seller\'s counsel as a required addition. Do not treat the absence of a Special Indemnity as a minor markup item; it is a **Critical** priority item that must be escalated to the responsible partner if the seller resists.
**[Section 7: Earnout Provisions]{.underline}**
**[7.1 General Guidance on Earnouts]{.underline}**

Earnout provisions in PE acquisitions are generally disfavored by the firm\'s PE buyer clients because they create ongoing economic entanglements with the seller, generate disputes over post-closing operations, and restrict the buyer\'s ability to integrate and restructure the acquired business. However, earnouts are sometimes commercially necessary to bridge a valuation gap between the buyer\'s and seller\'s expectations of the target\'s future performance. When an earnout is commercially required, it must be structured carefully to preserve the buyer\'s operational flexibility post-closing.
**[7.2 Buyer\'s Operational Covenants During Earnout Period]{.underline}**

**THIS IS A HIGH-PRIORITY REQUIREMENT.** Earnout provisions MUST NOT contain any affirmative operational covenant requiring the buyer to operate the acquired business \"in a manner consistent with past practice,\" \"in a manner designed to maximize the Earnout Payment,\" \"in substantially the same manner as operated prior to the Closing,\" or similar language that would restrict the buyer\'s ability to integrate, restructure, make capital investments, change pricing strategies, adjust compensation structures, enter new markets, exit underperforming lines of business, or otherwise operate the acquired business as the buyer sees fit in its sole discretion.

**Acceptable Standard.** The only covenant the firm will accept regarding the buyer\'s post-closing conduct in relation to an earnout is a narrow negative covenant providing that the buyer will not take any action with the **primary purpose** of reducing or avoiding the Earnout Payment. This carefully calibrated formulation achieves the appropriate balance of interests:

**Specific Instruction.** If the seller\'s draft includes language requiring the buyer to operate the business \"in a manner consistent with past practice and in good faith to maximize the Earnout Payment,\" or similar language imposing affirmative operational obligations, this MUST be struck and replaced with the narrow \"primary purpose\" negative covenant. The associate should provide a margin comment explaining the firm\'s position and the rationale for the change. **Priority: HIGH.**
**Sample Acceptable Earnout Covenant Language:**

> *\"Following the Closing, Buyer shall not, and shall cause the Company not to, take any action with the primary purpose of reducing or avoiding the Earnout Payment. For the avoidance of doubt, nothing in this Section \[\_\_\] shall restrict Buyer\'s right to operate, integrate, restructure, or otherwise manage the Company and its business in Buyer\'s sole discretion, including without limitation the right to make capital expenditure decisions, pricing changes, personnel decisions, strategic investments, acquisitions, dispositions, organizational restructurings, and operational modifications, and no such action shall constitute a breach of this Section \[\_\_\] unless taken with the primary purpose of reducing or avoiding the Earnout Payment.\"*

**Definition of Adjusted EBITDA for Earnout Purposes.** The definition of Adjusted EBITDA used for the earnout calculation should be precisely defined in the SPA and should include add-backs for the following categories of items to prevent manipulation claims in either direction:
> \(e\) Intercompany charges from the buyer or its affiliates to the target that were not charged on a consistent basis prior to the closing.

Representations and warranties insurance (\"R&W Insurance\") is increasingly standard in PE acquisitions in the environmental services sector, particularly for transactions with enterprise values above \$100 million. The buyer typically procures a buy-side R&W Insurance policy to supplement (not replace) the seller\'s direct indemnification obligations under the SPA. The buy-side policy provides the buyer with a direct claim against the insurer for losses arising from breaches of the seller\'s representations and warranties, subject to the policy\'s terms, conditions, exclusions, retentions, and limits.

Common providers of R&W Insurance in recent environmental services transactions handled by the firm include Granite Ridge Underwriters and similar specialty insurers with experience in the environmental sector. The premium for a buy-side policy is typically 2.5% to 4.0% of the policy limit, paid by the buyer at closing. The policy limit is typically set at the general indemnification cap under the SPA.

**Key Policy Exclusions.** R&W Insurance policies in environmental services transactions typically include exclusions for: (a) known matters (i.e., matters specifically identified in the due diligence process or disclosed on the seller\'s disclosure schedules); (b) environmental liabilities (or, in some cases, sub-limits for environmental liabilities rather than a complete exclusion); (c) specific pre-identified risks flagged by the insurer during underwriting; and (d) forward-looking statements and projections.

These exclusions underscore the critical importance of the Special Indemnity provisions described in Section 6. Because the R&W Insurance policy will typically exclude or sub-limit coverage for known environmental liabilities, the seller\'s direct indemnification through the Special Indemnity is the buyer\'s primary source of protection for specifically identified environmental exposures. The R&W Insurance policy and the Special Indemnity serve complementary but distinct functions, and both must be in place.

**THIS IS A HIGH-PRIORITY REQUIREMENT.** Where the buyer is obtaining R&W Insurance, the SPA MUST include a provision waiving the R&W insurer\'s subrogation rights against the seller, except in cases of seller fraud.

**Standard Formulation.** The SPA should provide that the buyer shall cause the R&W Insurance policy to include a provision waiving the insurer\'s right of subrogation against the seller and its affiliates, directors, officers, employees, and representatives, except to the extent any losses arise from or relate to fraud committed by the seller. The waiver should run to the benefit of the seller and its related parties and should be irrevocable for the term of the policy.

**Rationale.** The subrogation waiver is a key commercial term in any R&W Insurance-backed transaction. Without the waiver, the R&W insurer --- after paying a claim to the buyer --- could \"step into the buyer\'s shoes\" and pursue subrogation claims against the seller to recover the amounts paid. This subrogation right would effectively nullify the benefit of R&W Insurance from the seller\'s perspective, because the seller would face the same indemnification exposure (now from the insurer rather than the buyer) that the insurance was supposed to address. The subrogation waiver eliminates this circular liability and is a standard market practice that sellers commonly require as a condition to agreeing to the overall indemnification structure, including the cap, basket, and escrow terms.

The exception for fraud preserves the insurer\'s (and the buyer\'s) rights against a seller who has committed fraud in connection with the transaction. A fraudulent seller is not entitled to the benefit of the subrogation waiver, and the insurer should retain full recourse against such a seller.

**Specific Instruction.** If the seller\'s draft SPA makes no reference to R&W Insurance or to the waiver of insurer subrogation rights, the associate must add an R&W Insurance subrogation waiver provision. In many transactions, the availability and structure of R&W Insurance is negotiated at the term-sheet level, and the subrogation waiver is a term-sheet-level commitment. Its omission from the SPA must be corrected. **Priority: HIGH.**

> *\"Buyer shall obtain and maintain a representations and warranties insurance policy (the \'R&W Insurance Policy\') and shall cause such R&W Insurance Policy to provide that the insurer thereunder shall waive, and shall not exercise or pursue, any right of subrogation or any other right of recovery against Seller or any of its Affiliates, directors, officers, employees, agents, or representatives with respect to any claim made by Buyer under such R&W Insurance Policy, except to the extent such claim arises from or relates to Fraud by Seller. Buyer shall not amend, modify, or waive any provision of the R&W Insurance Policy in a manner that would adversely affect Seller\'s rights under this Section \[\_\_\] without Seller\'s prior written consent.\"*

**Coordination with Other Provisions.** The availability of R&W Insurance does not change the SPA\'s indemnification cap, escrow requirements, or other indemnification terms. The R&W Insurance policy is a supplement to the seller\'s direct indemnification obligations, not a substitute for them. Associates should resist any seller argument that the availability of R&W Insurance justifies a lower SPA indemnification cap or a smaller escrow.

The SPA must include a standard net working capital (\"NWC\") true-up mechanism to ensure that the target is delivered to the buyer at closing with a normalized level of working capital. The firm\'s standard NWC adjustment mechanics are as follows:

The SPA must require the seller to deliver payoff letters from each holder of target indebtedness no later than three (3) business days prior to the scheduled closing date. Each payoff letter must include: (a) the total outstanding balance as of the anticipated closing date (including accrued and unpaid interest, prepayment premiums, breakage costs, and all other amounts necessary to fully satisfy the obligation); (b) wiring instructions for the payoff amount; and (c) an agreement by the lender to deliver lien release documentation (including UCC-3 termination statements, mortgage releases, and intellectual property lien releases, as applicable) promptly upon receipt of the payoff amount.

Delivery of payoff letters meeting these requirements should be a condition to the buyer\'s obligation to close. If payoff letters are not delivered timely, the buyer should have the right to delay closing until they are delivered or, if the delay exceeds a specified number of business days, to terminate the agreement.
> \(c\) All capital lease obligations (determined in accordance with GAAP);

**Lender Coordination.** The buyer\'s acquisition lender (e.g., Clearwater Environmental Lending Corp. or a similar specialty lender) will typically require payoff letters as a condition to funding the acquisition facility. The SPA\'s closing mechanics must align with the lender\'s requirements regarding the timing and content of payoff letters. Associates should obtain and review the buyer\'s lender\'s commitment letter to identify any specific payoff letter requirements and ensure that the SPA\'s closing conditions are consistent.

Non-competition and non-solicitation covenants are standard in PE acquisitions and are critical to protecting the buyer\'s investment in the acquired business. A well-drafted non-compete prevents the seller (and its principals) from establishing or participating in a competing business that could divert customers, employees, or business opportunities from the acquired company during the critical post-acquisition integration period.

Associates should always cross-reference the executed term sheet for the agreed-upon non-compete parameters (duration, geographic scope, and business scope). The SPA\'s non-compete provisions must conform to the term sheet.

**Duration.** Two (2) to four (4) years post-closing. Three (3) years is the most common duration in recent environmental services transactions handled by the firm and is the firm\'s standard recommendation. Durations shorter than two years provide inadequate protection for the buyer\'s investment; durations longer than four years may raise enforceability concerns in certain jurisdictions.

**Geographic Scope.** The non-compete should be limited to the states and jurisdictions in which the target conducts business as of the closing date, plus any states or jurisdictions in which the target has active proposals or bids pending as of the closing date. A nationwide non-compete is generally not advisable unless the target operates in a majority of states. An overbroad geographic restriction risks unenforceability --- courts in many jurisdictions will decline to enforce a non-compete with a geographic scope that is not reasonably tailored to the legitimate business interest being protected.

**Business Scope.** The non-compete should be limited to the specific business lines of the target --- for example, \"environmental remediation services, hazardous waste management and transportation services, and environmental consulting and engineering services.\" The non-compete should not extend to \"any business\" or to business lines unrelated to the target\'s operations. Where the seller is a diversified holding company with business lines unrelated to the target (e.g., construction, timber management, real estate development), an overbroad non-compete could restrict legitimate seller activities and may be struck down by a court as unreasonable in its scope.

**Enforceability Considerations.** Enforceability of non-compete covenants varies significantly by jurisdiction. Delaware courts generally enforce reasonable non-competition covenants entered into in connection with the sale of a business, applying a reasonableness standard that considers the duration, geographic scope, and business scope of the restriction in light of the legitimate interests being protected. Oregon courts similarly apply a reasonableness test but impose specific statutory requirements for non-compete agreements. Some jurisdictions (most notably California) are hostile to non-compete covenants generally, although the sale-of-business exception may apply. Associates should identify the governing law of the non-compete provision and confirm that the covenant\'s terms are consistent with the requirements of that jurisdiction. Overbroad covenants risk being voided entirely rather than judicially reformed, depending on the jurisdiction\'s approach to reformation (sometimes called \"blue penciling\").

**Non-Solicitation.** In addition to the non-compete, the SPA should include non-solicitation covenants prohibiting the seller and its principals from (a) soliciting or hiring employees of the target and (b) soliciting or diverting customers or suppliers of the target. The non-solicitation period should match the non-compete period.

**Firm Standard.** For targets with fewer than 500 employees (which includes the majority of environmental services targets in the middle-market range), actual knowledge of the Chief Executive Officer and Chief Financial Officer (or their functional equivalents) is an acceptable Knowledge standard. These individuals typically have sufficient familiarity with the target\'s operations, financial condition, regulatory compliance status, and material contracts to provide meaningful knowledge-qualified representations.

This section provides guidance on provisions that, while potentially appearing sub-optimal from the buyer\'s perspective, are within acceptable market ranges and should generally NOT be marked up in the seller\'s draft. Disciplined markup is essential to maintaining the credibility of the associate, the responsible partner, and the firm. Marking up provisions that are squarely within market range wastes negotiating capital, creates unnecessary friction, and signals to the seller\'s counsel that the buyer\'s team is either inexperienced or unreasonable.

> **Basket/Deductible at 0.75%--1.0% of Enterprise Value.** As discussed in Section 5.2, this is within the firm\'s acceptable range for middle-market environmental services transactions. A basket at 1.0% of enterprise value should not be marked up. Do not attempt to negotiate the basket down to 0.5% or lower merely because a lower basket would be better for the buyer --- the improvement is marginal and the negotiating capital is better spent elsewhere.

In a stock acquisition, the target entity itself does not change --- the same legal entity that held the environmental permits before the transaction continues to hold them after the transaction. This is one of the principal advantages of a stock purchase structure for environmental services targets with complex permitting portfolios. However, the mere fact that the permit-holding entity does not change does not mean that the change of control is transparent to regulators.

Many state environmental regulatory programs --- including programs authorized under RCRA, the Clean Air Act, and the Clean Water Act --- require notification to, or approval from, the issuing regulatory agency upon a change of control of the permit holder, even in stock purchase transactions. The specific requirements vary by state and by permit type, and failure to comply with applicable notification or approval requirements can result in permit violations, enforcement actions, or, in extreme cases, permit revocation.

**States of Particular Note.** Based on the firm\'s recent transaction experience in the environmental services sector, the following states impose change-of-control notification or approval requirements that are particularly relevant:

> \(a\) **Oregon:** The Oregon Department of Environmental Quality (\"DEQ\") requires change-of-ownership notifications for certain categories of environmental permits, including RCRA hazardous waste facility permits and water quality permits.
> \(b\) **Washington:** The Washington Department of Ecology requires similar notifications and, in some cases, formal approval for changes of ownership affecting certain environmental permits.

> \(c\) **California:** The California Department of Toxic Substances Control (\"DTSC\") has specific requirements for notification and, in certain circumstances, prior approval of changes of control for hazardous waste facility permits.
> \(d\) **Nevada:** The Nevada Division of Environmental Protection (\"NDEP\") imposes change-of-ownership notification requirements for certain permits.

**Firm Standard.** The SPA should include both (a) a representation regarding the current status of all Environmental Permits held by the target (including confirmation that all permits are in full force and effect, that no permit is subject to pending revocation or suspension, and that no conditions exist that could give rise to revocation or suspension) AND (b) pre-closing and post-closing covenants requiring the seller\'s cooperation in the notification, transfer, or re-issuance of Environmental Permits as required by applicable law. The cooperation covenant should extend through a period of at least twelve (12) months post-closing to cover permits with longer regulatory processing timelines.

Associates should review the environmental due diligence memo for a comprehensive list of all target permits and should flag any permits that require transfer notifications or regulatory approvals in connection with the change of control.

Environmental services companies frequently derive a significant portion of their revenue from government contracts --- including federal, state, and local contracts --- for environmental remediation, environmental consulting, environmental monitoring, and related services. Government contracts present unique legal issues in the acquisition context that associates must address in the SPA.

**Federal Government Contracts.** Federal government contracts are subject to the Anti-Assignment Act (41 U.S.C. § 6305), which generally prohibits the assignment of government contracts without the consent of the contracting officer. In addition, FAR 42.12 sets forth the procedures for novation agreements when a contractor undergoes a change of ownership. A novation agreement is a three-party agreement among the government, the original contractor, and the successor contractor, pursuant to which the government recognizes the successor as the contractor under the existing contract.

Even in stock purchase transactions --- where the contracting entity does not change --- certain changes in ownership may trigger novation or recognition requirements under FAR. Specifically, FAR 42.1204 provides that a novation agreement may be required when a contractor is acquired by another entity, even if the contractor entity continues to exist. The determination of whether a novation is required depends on the circumstances, including whether the contractor entity remains intact and continues to perform under the contract.

> \(i\) A representation regarding the status of all government contracts held by the target, including confirmation that all contracts are in good standing, that no contracts are subject to pending termination for default or convenience, and that no debarment or suspension proceedings are pending or threatened;

> \(ii\) A pre-closing covenant requiring the seller and the target to use commercially reasonable efforts to obtain novation or recognition agreements from applicable government contracting officers, to the extent required by applicable law or regulation; and

> \(iii\) Consideration of whether government contract consent should be a closing condition. For targets where government contracts represent a material portion of revenue (typically more than 20%), the failure to obtain required novation agreements may justify a closing condition. For targets with a smaller government contract exposure, a pre-closing covenant with commercially reasonable efforts may be sufficient.

Associates should cross-reference the government contracts section of the due diligence memo and consult with the firm\'s Government Contracts Practice Group for guidance on specific novation requirements.

> \(a\) **Accuracy of Representations and Warranties.** The seller\'s representations and warranties must be true and correct as of the closing date as though made on such date (with appropriate exceptions for representations made as of a specific date). For non-Fundamental Representations, accuracy is qualified by a Material Adverse Effect standard (i.e., the representations must be true and correct except where the failure to be true and correct would not, individually or in the aggregate, reasonably be expected to have a Material Adverse Effect). For Fundamental Representations, accuracy must be true and correct in all respects (other than de minimis inaccuracies).
> \(c\) **No Material Adverse Effect.** No Material Adverse Effect shall have occurred since the date of the agreement.
In addition to the standard closing conditions set forth in Section 13.1, the following sector-specific closing conditions should be included in environmental services acquisitions where applicable:

> \(a\) **Government Contract Novation or Recognition.** Where the target holds material government contracts that require novation or recognition agreements in connection with the change of control, the receipt of such novation or recognition agreements (or, at minimum, written confirmation from the applicable contracting officer that the novation process is underway and that interim performance will be permitted) should be a closing condition. See Section 12.2 for further guidance.

> \(b\) **Environmental Permit Transfer Notifications.** Where applicable state law requires notification to or approval from a regulatory agency in connection with a change of control of the permit holder, confirmation that all required notifications have been filed (and, where prior approval is required, that such approval has been obtained) should be a closing condition. See Section 12.1 for further guidance.

> \(c\) **No New Environmental Claims.** Confirmation that no new material environmental claim, enforcement action, notice of violation, CERCLA information request, or similar regulatory action has been received by the target since the date of the agreement that would, individually or in the aggregate, reasonably be expected to have a Material Adverse Effect.

> \(d\) **Environmental Impairment Liability Insurance.** Confirmation that all environmental impairment liability insurance policies maintained by the target remain in full force and effect as of the closing date, with coverage levels no less than those in effect as of the date of the agreement.

The following checklist summarizes all critical and high-priority items covered in this playbook. Associates should use this checklist as a quick-reference guide when performing markup of a seller\'s draft SPA in an environmental services transaction. Each item includes a priority designation and a cross-reference to the relevant section of this playbook for detailed guidance.

1\. **MAE Definition --- Disproportionate Impact Qualifier** \[CRITICAL\]. Confirm that all industry-specific and regulatory carve-outs in the MAE definition include a \"disproportionate impact\" qualifier. If the carve-out for \"changes in the environmental services industry generally\" or \"changes in environmental laws or regulations\" lacks the qualifier, flag and correct immediately. *(Ref. Section 2.1)*

2\. **Interim Covenants --- Affiliate Transaction Restriction** \[HIGH\]. Confirm that the interim operating covenants include a specific restriction prohibiting the target from entering into, amending, extending, or terminating any affiliate transaction without buyer\'s prior written consent. *(Ref. Section 3.2)*

3\. **Indemnification Cap --- Conformity with Term Sheet** \[CRITICAL\]. Confirm that the general indemnification cap matches the percentage agreed in the executed term sheet (typical range: 10%--15% of enterprise value; firm standard: 12.5%). Flag and correct any deviation from the term sheet. *(Ref. Section 5.1)*

4\. **Environmental Representation Survival --- Minimum 36 Months** \[CRITICAL\]. Confirm that environmental representations survive for a minimum of 36 months post-closing, carved out from the general representation survival period. Preferred position: full statute of limitations. *(Ref. Section 4.2)*

5\. **Pro-Sandbagging Clause** \[CRITICAL\]. Confirm that the SPA contains an affirmative pro-sandbagging provision. If the seller\'s draft contains an anti-sandbagging clause, strike it and replace with pro-sandbagging language. *(Ref. Section 5.3)*

6\. **Special Indemnity for Known Environmental Liabilities** \[CRITICAL\]. Confirm that a Special Indemnity is included for each identified environmental liability with estimated exposure of \$1,000,000 or more; 72-month survival; dollar-one recovery (outside the basket); not subject to the general cap. *(Ref. Section 6)*

7\. **Earnout Operational Covenants --- No Affirmative Obligations** \[HIGH\]. Confirm that earnout provisions do not contain affirmative operational covenants (e.g., \"operate in a manner consistent with past practice\" or \"maximize the Earnout Payment\"). Only the narrow \"primary purpose\" negative covenant is acceptable. *(Ref. Section 7.2)*
8\. **R&W Insurance Subrogation Waiver** \[HIGH\]. Confirm that the SPA includes a waiver of the R&W insurer\'s subrogation rights against the seller (except for fraud). *(Ref. Section 8.2)*

9\. **Payoff Letters as Closing Condition** \[HIGH\]. Confirm that the SPA requires delivery of payoff letters from all holders of target indebtedness at least 3 business days prior to closing, and that delivery is a condition to buyer\'s obligation to close. *(Ref. Section 9.2)*

10\. **Non-Compete Scope** \[MEDIUM-HIGH\]. Confirm that non-compete provisions match the term sheet in duration, geographic scope, and business scope. Avoid overbroad restrictions that could capture seller\'s unrelated business activities or that risk unenforceability. *(Ref. Section 10.1)*

11\. **Government Contract Novation** \[HIGH\]. Confirm that the SPA addresses Anti-Assignment Act and FAR novation requirements, including representations, pre-closing covenants, and (where applicable) closing conditions for material government contracts. *(Ref. Section 12.2)*

12\. **Environmental Permit Transfer Covenants** \[HIGH\]. Confirm that the SPA includes cooperation covenants for environmental permit notifications and transfers required by applicable state law in connection with the change of control. *(Ref. Section 12.1)*

4.2                     October 2025            Current version. Updated R&W Insurance guidance; revised earnout covenant standards; added government contract novation guidance; updated market data for indemnification caps and EBITDA multiples.
4.1                     March 2025              Updated Special Indemnity survival period guidance; added Section 12.2 (government contracts); minor formatting corrections.
